2025-10-16, the partnership terms page of 2025-10-15 and the Launch YC post of 2025-10-19. Anything later is under

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.instead: Holding up on all 4 of 4 beliefs from 7 agents, the narrowest being Importance and Current solution at 6 of 7 against a bar of 5. That is a small group, so treat the problem as a go to test the solution next, not as proof of the seven-figure loss.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7", so I can see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip has seven cells, all for me, on a 0 to 7 axis, with the marker at 6 labelled "at least 8 in 10", so what is counted, over whom and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: My circumstance was that booking calls come in on every shift and not every one gets answered, but the card drops the unanswered part, so it tests something any reservation agent says yes to.
screens.why_b4: "How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards" points me onward, but it doesn't say whether missed calls are common, which is what my pitch rests on.
screens.why_b5: The count line shows n=7 and calls it "a small group: a lean, not a call", and "Common among these 7" stays inside the people who answered.
screens.instead: Ask whether a booking call rang out unanswered on their shift in the last 7 days, and show how many of the 7 said yes against my 8 in 10.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 inside what you said · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The day axis reads '0 1 2 3 4 5 6 median 7', which jams the median label between 6 and 7, and the legend runs together as 'what you said at what you said short of it'; the bar '5 of 7' also reads as people on a days-out-of-7 axis, so I had to look twice to see that 5 means people, not 5 days.
screens.why_b3: 'Booking call come in on their shift on 5 to 7 days out of 7' is the band I set for my reservation agents, and the card is called Frequency.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' only sends me on; it does not say that calls come in on nearly every shift, so the missed-call exposure is daily and the pain question is what counts now.
screens.why_b5: The card shows '7 answered · 7 counted' with 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it does not claim more than 6 of 7 can carry.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 agents take booking calls on nearly every shift (median 6 days), so missed calls can hit you any day; from 7 people that is a lean, so check next whether those missed calls hurt enough to matter.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that clears my bar together, though the count line is printed twice.
screens.why_b2: The caption says the bars count 14 picks from 7 people, but the strip, which should be one cell per person, shows 6 for and 8 against with my marker at 5, so I have to stop and work out that it is counting picks, not people.
screens.why_b3: The title Importance and the belief line are word for word the ones I checked: five hard things across a week of shifts, unanswered booking calls one of the two.
screens.why_b4: The So line properly warns that this means top two, not first, but it doesn't tell me what to do next, and it ignores what Chiara's quote points to: groups whose call center already covers after six may not be my buyer.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown and called "a lean, not a call", but the other bars and the strip are labelled "against" (8), even though only Chiara left my problem out of her two; the other picks came mostly from people who count for me, so the chart makes the opposition look bigger than it is.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 agents put unanswered booking calls in their top two (bar 5 of 7, a lean on 7 people); the one who didn't has a call center covering after six, so lead with groups that have no after-hours cover. Draw the strip one cell per person: 6 for, 1 against.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Five rungs, a count on each, for or against marked, the line drawn under "A few rang out, all called back that day", and the strip shows 6 for against 1 with the marker at 5; it reads in one look.
screens.why_b3: The title "Current solution" and the belief about the central office or call center still falling short are word for word what I checked.
screens.why_b4: "Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study" names the next step, but it doesn't say what the gap means for me; 4 of 7 at "many rang out" or worse is a bigger leak than my 5% pitch, and the screen leaves that unsaid.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible as "6 of these 7", the small group is called "a lean, not a call", and Chiara's answer against is shown, not hidden.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean on 7: for 4 of the 7 most calls that rang out were never called back, which is worse than the 5% you pitch, so lead the solution study with the calls lost after hours and at peak.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits beside '6 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it in one line.
screens.why_b3: The box is named Importance and carries my belief word for word: five hard things across a week of shifts, with unanswered booking calls in the top two.
screens.why_b4: 'Importance held, 6 of 7; the 1 who said no' only repeats the result; the screen never says what the one dissent means for me, for example that groups whose call center already covers after six are a weaker segment, and it is silent on the Current solution line I also checked.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible everywhere ('1 against · 1 asked their why here', 'On their own (1)'), and nothing claims more than one person said.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's quote tells me something I did not type: where the call center covers after six, the pain moves to group emails with no rates attached and rates across channels, which are competing jobs I could lose the top-two slot to.
screens.instead: Importance held 6 of 7; the one against has a call center covering after six and is losing time to group emails and rates instead, so test whether call-center-covered groups belong in your segment. Current solution's one against is shown here too, or the screen says why it isn't.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is the obvious gate: it checks that I'm the person the study is for before asking about my calls.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call centre are everyday words in my job at a Munich hotel group, and I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know where I work and that our group runs a central reservations office, so it's an easy yes.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover a gate question completely, and the guidelines give a gate no escape, so none is missing.
screens.why5: It repeats the founder's segment in plain trade words and gives away nothing of a product or plan.
screens.why6: The stem is one short question that is easy to hold, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' sounds stiff for a yes-or-no gate, where just 'Yes or no.' would say better.
screens.instead: Do you work at a hotel group in Germany that runs a central reservations office or call centre? Yes or no.

screens.why1: A gate makes sense here, but for someone who takes booking calls all shift, and on a trade-fair Saturday nonstop, 'did a booking call come in' is a given, so it filters nobody out.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words and I'd answer instantly.
screens.why3: It's exactly my job and I know the answer without thinking.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but the gate shows two escape chips: 'I'd rather not say' isn't meant to exist and a gate should have none, and 'I can't recall one particular call' is nonsense when I took hundreds this week.
screens.why5: It stays with calls coming in on my shift, with nothing about a product or anyone's plan reaching me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered or get dropped? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: It follows the gate naturally, but in a Munich reservations office booking calls come in on every single shift, so the answer is just the number of days I worked, which tells nobody much.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly which days I worked last week, the trade-fair Saturday included, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: One to seven covers every case after the gate, the numbers can't overlap, and I can't recall fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the hard part of the job is the calls that don't get answered at peak, and this counts only calls coming in, so the point drifted.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and saying a number from 1 to 7 or that you can't recall is easy to hold and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did a booking call on your shift go unanswered? Say a number from 0 to 7, or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: After asking how many days booking calls came in, it makes sense to ask which part of my shift I would most want made easier.
screens.why2: Every option is in words we use in the office (rates, channels, group requests, calls ringing out), so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly what wears me down on a trade-fair Saturday, so I can answer this from my own last week.
screens.why4: In a central reservations office I never stand at a desk or work the check-in rush, so two of the five are not my job, and what actually hits us at peak is missing: too many calls waiting at once.
screens.why5: The unanswered booking calls sit plainly among ordinary tasks without naming any product, so the founder's point is kept and nothing leaks.
screens.why6: One short question and five short, parallel options with one escape at the end, so I can hold it when I hear it once.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of shifts. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Too many calls waiting at once; booking calls that ring out unanswered; answering booking emails and group requests; checking availability across our hotels; or keeping rates right on every channel. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: Asking how ring-outs were handled fits after picking what I'd like easier, but it opens on my last single call and then asks about many calls, which is abrupt.
screens.why2: I have to read it twice: 'my last call' and 'many rang out' don't go together, and 'through a central reservations office or call center' is a clumsy way to describe where I already work.
screens.why3: I know what happened to calls that rang out on my own shifts, but one last call has no 'some' or 'many', so I'd be guessing which time it means.
screens.why4: The ladder is mostly clear, but 'some rang out, called back when there was time' and 'many rang out, few were called back' blur together, and 'Someone else did it' is an odd escape for me, the agent answering.
screens.why5: 'Answering booking calls through a central reservations office or call center' is the screener's segment wording dropped back in, not how anyone in our office talks, though it doesn't give away a product.
screens.why6: Five short options I can hold, but the long 'central reservations office or call center' clause is a mouthful heard, and the single-call anchor fights the options.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. What happened to the booking calls nobody could pick up? -- All called back within minutes; all called back the same day; some called back when there was time; most never called back; or say I can't recall.
